linkedin_post:
Time blocking works best when your calendar and your task list stop living in separate places.

Notion Calendar lets you see both in one week view: recurring time blocks from Google Calendar, plus tasks from a Notion database with a Do date. Here's a setup that takes about 20 minutes:

1. Use four block types (deep work, admin, meetings, recovery) with colors you never change.
2. Build a recurring template week and leave 1–2 hours a day unblocked.
3. Mark focus blocks as Busy and meeting windows as Free, so colleagues book you when you actually want meetings.
4. Give tasks a Do date with a time so they land inside the right block.
5. Once the template exists, move tasks, not blocks.

Then protect a 10-minute weekly plan: review last week, lock in commitments, schedule your top three outcomes into deep work blocks and check each day for overload.

If your role is reactive or you're on call, anchor blocks or theme days are often a better fit than planning every hour.

Full step-by-step guide, including the Tasks database properties and views: {URL}

reddit_title: A time-blocking setup in Notion Calendar that holds up when your week gets messy (full steps, ~20 min)
reddit_post:
**Short version:** Connect Google Calendar to Notion Calendar. Create recurring, color-coded events for four block types. Add a Notion tasks database so tasks with a date and time show up inside those blocks. Then spend about 10 minutes a week assigning tasks to blocks. The first setup takes about 20 minutes.

**1. Connect your calendars (3 min)**
Install Notion Calendar, sign in with your Notion account and connect Google. If you have separate work and personal Google accounts, connect both so you see your whole week in one view. Notion Calendar was built around Google Calendar, and support for Outlook and Apple has changed over time. Check Notion's help center for the current list before you build anything.

**2. Four block types, fixed colors (3 min)**
- Deep work (e.g. blue)
- Admin (yellow)
- Meetings (purple)
- Recovery (green)

Never change the colors. Your primary Google Calendar is the simplest place to keep the blocks, and blocks there usually show as busy. A separate calendar for each type is easy to hide, but those events may not show as busy to colleagues. Write your colors and rules down on a Notion page.

**3. Template week (5 min)**
In week view, drag to create a block (e.g. "Deep work," Mon 8:30–10:30) and set it to repeat. Add:
- a daily admin block
- recovery blocks after deep work and at lunch
- meeting windows on 2–3 afternoons

Leave 1–2 hours a day unblocked as flex time.

**4. Busy/Free, privacy, reminders (2 min)**
- Deep work, admin and recovery → Busy
- Meeting windows → Free, so people book you when you *want* meetings
- Client or project names in titles → set visibility to Private
- Turn off reminders you don't need

If Notion Calendar doesn't have a setting, change it in the event's details in Google Calendar.

**5. Tasks database (5 min)**
Properties:
- Name
- Status (Not started / In progress / Done)
- Block type (Select with the same four options, in matching colors)
- Do date (Date)
- Estimate (Select: 15 / 30 / 60 / 90 min)

Views:
- "Unscheduled": Do date is empty and Status is not Done
- "This week": a board grouped by Block type, using the relative date filter for this week's Do dates

**6. Add the database to Notion Calendar (2 min)**
Connect your workspace, add the Tasks database and pick Do date as the date property. Any task with a Do date now appears on the calendar, and dragging it to a new slot updates its date in Notion.

**7. Test it (1 min)**
Give one task a Do date with "Include time" turned on, set to a time inside a matching block. If it shows up as an all-day item, the time isn't included. This is the most common snag.

**8. The 10-minute weekly plan (Sunday or Friday)**
Review last week → lock in fixed commitments → put your top 3 outcomes into deep work blocks → batch small tasks into admin blocks → check that every day still has recovery and flex time → rename Monday's first block after its task.

**Rules that keep it working**
- Once the template is built, move tasks, not blocks.
- If you miss a block, drag it to the next open slot instead of deleting it. Your weekly review will then show patterns, like a block that always gets interrupted, so you can move it in the template.
- Block length: many people find 60–120 min deep work blocks plus a 15–30 min recovery block work well. If you're new to this, start with one 60-minute deep work block a day.
- If your work is reactive, you're on call or you have young kids, use a few anchor blocks or theme days instead of planning every hour.

**No Notion Calendar?** Add a calendar view to the Tasks database and give each task a start and end time. The downside is that you generally won't see your Google Calendar meetings next to them.

**Cost:** Notion Calendar has generally come at no extra cost with a Notion account, but pricing can change. Check Notion's pricing page, especially if you're on a work workspace with its own admin settings.

Full disclosure: this is condensed from a longer guide on my site, The Wealth Ascent, which also has FAQs on color-coding and missed blocks: {URL}. You shouldn't need it to set this up, though; everything is above. Happy to answer questions about the database setup.
pinterest_title: Time Block Your Week in Notion Calendar: 20-Minute Setup with 4 Color-Coded Blocks
pinterest_description: Learn how to time block your week in Notion Calendar with four color-coded block types: deep work, admin, meetings and recovery. Connect Google Calendar, build a recurring template week and link a Notion tasks database so your to-dos land inside the right blocks. Finish with a simple 10-minute weekly planning routine that keeps your schedule realistic.
